turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, nice to meet you too. I guess I'm here because I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Important stuff, you know? Like my heart follow-up appointments, or remembering to call the clinic back. 

Speaking of that clinic, they have this absolute racket they play for their hold music. It’s this smooth jazz saxophone that just loops every thirty seconds. It drives me up the wall, but it actually reminds me of this little club my buddy Lou used to drag me to back in the 80s. Lou played the trumpet, actually. Not professionally, but he was pretty good. We used to go down there on Tuesdays... wait, maybe it was Thursdays? They had 50-cent wings on Thursdays. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, forgetting things. Yeah, it's not just the doctors. Like the other day, I went over to help my neighbor with a repair job on his back deck, and I showed up without any of the right tools! I was standing there empty-handed. Just completely slipped my mind. So, yeah, that's what brings me in.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly states they keep forgetting important daily activities, such as medical appointments, returning phone calls to the clinic, and bringing the necessary tools for a repair job.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates tangential speech, drifting from the topic of the clinic to hold music, a friend named Lou, playing the trumpet, and 50-cent wings, before losing their train of thought and asking what they were saying.

turns.doctor_question: Are you still able to manage your bills and medications on your own?
turns.patient_response:
Bills and medications? Uh, I'm not really sure, I haven't really noticed any big issues with that, I guess. I just kind of toss the mail on the kitchen counter when it comes. 

Speaking of the mail, they completely changed our route times recently. We used to get it right at 11 AM, like clockwork. Now it's just whenever they feel like it. The regular guy, Gary, he retired a few months back. Great guy. He used to drive this old Chevy Nova on his days off. Beautiful car, cherry red. I had a buddy in high school with a Nova, and we used to take it down to the lake on weekends. We'd fish for bass for hours. Never caught much, but it was a good time, you know? I haven't been fishing in years, though. I should really get my old tackle box out of the garage... but man, that garage is an absolute disaster area right now. I was supposed to organize it last spring and just never got around to it. 

Anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the bills and stuff. Yeah, I don't know, I guess I get to them eventually when they're sitting right in front of me.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly mentions that their garage is a 'disaster area' and that they have failed to organize it despite intending to do so.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech and derailment, drifting from the topic of mail to the mailman, cars, fishing, and their garage before forgetting the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Do you need help managing your medications?
turns.patient_response:
Help with my meds? No, I don't think so. I just take them myself. I keep the bottles right next to the toaster so I see them when I'm making breakfast. 

I've been eating the exact same thing for breakfast for, oh, it's gotta be twenty years now. Two slices of sourdough toast and orange marmalade. You know, they actually stopped selling the good brand of marmalade at my local grocery store. The one with the little gingham lid? Now it's all that cheap high-fructose stuff. I tried complaining to the manager—young kid, couldn't have been older than nineteen. Nice enough kid, but he looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Kids today just don't get customer service, do they? 

Back when I worked at the hardware store right out of high school, we would walk the customer right to the exact aisle if they needed something. We had these heavy green aprons with the big pockets for nails and screws. My buddy Dale and I used to see who could ring up a register the fastest... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the pills. Yeah, no, nobody helps me with them, I just do it myself.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about breakfast and past jobs, causing them to lose track of and forget the doctor's initial question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling monologue about marmalade and a hardware store in response to a simple yes/no question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you missed paying any bills because you forgot?
turns.patient_response:
Missed paying bills? Well, like I said earlier, I just kind of leave them on the counter. But honestly, that's exactly the kind of thing I'm talking about. The forgetting. It's why I came in today. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting at my age. 

Like my heart doctor—I'm supposed to have these follow-up appointments, and I just completely blank on them. Or I'll tell myself I need to call the clinic back, and then... nothing. Poof. Gone from my brain. 

It's just like that deck repair I was telling you about with my neighbor. Showing up without the right tools! I mean, I used to work at a hardware store, for crying out loud. You'd think I'd know better. We used to sell these beautiful Craftsman tool sets back then. Real heavy-duty steel, not like the cheap plastic handles they make everything with now. I bought my first set with my third paycheck. Kept it in the trunk of my car for years. 

Actually, I think my son has that set now. He lives out in Colorado. Beautiful out there, the mountains and all. He went out there for college and just never came back east. He likes to hike... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, the bills. Yeah, the forgetting is just... it's getting to be a real problem with the important stuff, like the doctors and the tools.

Speaking of fruit, I bought these peaches the other day from that little stand out on Route 9. You know the one? The guy with the overalls always sits out there reading a paperback. Anyway, they looked great, but they were hard as rocks. I left them in a paper bag to ripen—my mother always swore by the paper bag trick. She used to can her own peaches every August. The whole house would smell like sugar and summer. We had this enormous copper pot she only brought out for canning season. I wonder whatever happened to that pot? My sister probably took it when they sold the house. She always had an eye for the antiques. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Someone taking over? No, no, it's just me handling the bills. For better or worse, I guess.

turns.doctor_question: Has your memory trouble caused your electricity, rent, or other bills to go unpaid?
turns.patient_response:
Unpaid? Well, I mean, they're late sometimes, sure, but I always get to them eventually. They don't shut the lights off or anything. I just wait until they send those pink envelopes, you know? The ones that say "Past Due" in big letters. 

I remember when the electric company used to send a guy out to actually read the meter on the side of the house. Our guy was named Frank. Big guy, always wore a gray uniform and carried this heavy flashlight, even in the middle of the day. He had a golden retriever that would sit in his truck while he did his rounds. Beautiful dog. Max, I think his name was. Or maybe Buster? No, Buster was the dog my uncle had when I was a kid. Buster was a terror, always digging up my aunt's petunias. She used to chase him around the yard with a rolled-up newspaper...

Oh, but no, they haven't shut anything off. I always manage to send a check before it gets to that point. I just... I need the pink envelopes to remind me.

Lost driving? No, no, I know my way around town just fine. I've been driving these roads for... gosh, forty years now?

turns.doctor_question: What month is it right now?
turns.patient_response:
Month? Oh, it's October. 

My favorite time of year, honestly. The leaves are just starting to turn over on Elm Street. We used to have this massive oak tree in our front yard when I was growing up. Every October, my dad would rake all the leaves into this huge pile, and my brother and I would jump in it until we were covered in dirt and little bits of dried leaves. My mother hated it because we'd track it all into the house. She had this vacuum—an old Hoover, heavy as a tank. Sounded like an airplane taking off. She'd be vacuuming and yelling over the noise about how we were turning her living room into a forest floor. 

My brother, he lives out in Arizona now. No autumn leaves out there, just rocks and cactus. I went to visit him a few years ago, and I swear, I don't know how he stands the heat. We went to this diner, and I ordered a slice of cherry pie... 

Wait, did you just need the month? Yeah, October.
